text: A customer just paid this invoice with PayPal. Watch the money reach the books, pay a supplier and land in the VAT return.
This is Accnomos. It keeps a UK small business's books in its own OneDrive or Google Drive, and files VAT to HMRC. PayPal is where the business gets paid, and where it pays its bills.

text: I add a PayPal payment link to an invoice. Accnomos creates a real PayPal invoice, in PayPal's sandbox, with the same lines and VAT, and puts the link on the PDF and in the email.
The customer pays in PayPal. This is PayPal's sandbox, so no real money moves.

PayPal's reports can lag by up to three hours, so here are payments from earlier today. Sync PayPal proposes each one: the gross, PayPal's fee and the net, matched to its invoice. A sale with no invoice waits until I choose its VAT. The AI suggests, code does the sums in pence, and nothing posts until I approve.
Then the tie-out: PayPal's own balance, with the time PayPal last refreshed it, against PayPal in my books, with the difference explained.

Bills work the other way. On a supplier bill's due date, Accnomos offers to pay it by PayPal Payout. I approve, and it posts when PayPal confirms. PayPal can't schedule a payout ahead, so Accnomos pays on or after the due date, when the app is open. Upcoming payments can go in my calendar.
If a customer opens a dispute, Accnomos builds the evidence from the books: the invoice, the payment and the dates, every figure checked by code. I read it before anything goes to PayPal.
And when the quarter ends, those PayPal sales are already in the VAT return, ready to file with HMRC's sandbox.
